**After Queen Victoria’s departure (her death on 22 January 1901), Buckingham Palace entered a deep period of mourning and then began a new chapter under her successor, King Edward VII.** | Phase | What happened | |-------|---------------| | **Mourning (early 1901)** | • The Royal Standard was lowered and the palace’s state apartments were shuttered.
• The public was barred from entry; the palace “went into the deepest court mourning that an English crown had ever known.”
• The palace’s doors remained closed during the funeral and memorial ceremonies for Victoria. | | **Transition to Edward VII (1901‑1902)** | • Edward VII visited the palace in March 1902 to perform the coronation honours ceremony.
• The palace was reopened for official use; the court moved from the “Marble Palace” on the grounds to the much larger, purpose‑built Buckingham building. | | **Redevelopment & Modernisation (1902‑1910)** | • Edward VII and Queen Alexandra commissioned a major Belle Époque–style refurbishment designed by architect Sir Edwin Lutyens.
• New electric lighting, plumbing, telephones, and other modern conveniences were installed.
• The state rooms were redecorated with the latest interior fashions and furnishings. | | **Historical Continuity & Use** | • Buckingham Palace became the main London residence and administrative headquarters for the monarch.
• It hosted royal court balls, diplomatic receptions, state visits, and national celebrations.
• The palace remained the centrepiece of the British monarchy’s public and ceremonial life—all the way through the 20th‑century upheavals (World Wars, post‑war restoration, the monarchy’s modern public outreach). | **Bottom line:** After Queen Victoria’s death, Buckingham Palace was closed for a short period of mourning, then revived under Edward VII, who presided over its first major refurbishment. Since then it has continued to function as the primary London residence of the sovereign and the epicentre of royal ceremony and state business.
